Before continuing with dDocent, checking the quality of the trimmed reads with FastQC

```{bash}
cd /home/ccaillon/RISG_dDocent_working

mkdir cleanedreads_fastqc_results
cd cleanedreads_fastqc_results

fastqc -o . /home/ccaillon/RISG_dDocent_working/*.R1.fq.gz
fastqc -o . /home/ccaillon/RISG_dDocent_working/*.R2.fq.gz
```

```{bash}
multiqc .
#Rename:
mv multiqc_report.html cleanedreads_multiqc_report.html
```

MultiQC report can be viewed here.
Everything looks good. All the sequences and adapter contents are in the green zone for quality check. All individuals have adapter content <1%, except MW_CB_3401 which does have higher adapter content but it's still a very small percentage (1.66%). MW_CB_3401 also have higher overrepresented sequences (red zone for quality check). It should not be problematic, since it's common for reduced representation sequencing to share common fragments. Keep an eye if these have significant impacts on MW_CB_3401 individual's downstream analyses.
Conclusion after meeting with Jon: More reads are linked to more adapter contents, and because these adapter contents are repetitive sequences it's also linked to higher overrepresented sequences. Typically, if a sample has more adapter content than others, that can means that the quality of the DNA was not as good going in, and so it ends up with shorter fragments. And the higher adapter content is linked to more overrepresented sequences because PCR biases favor smaller fragments. Jon confirms this is not a concern to have such low levels of adapter contents (2% or less) for downstream analyses.

## Read Mapping

Make sure reference.fasta file is in the directory.

Run dDocent again for Read Mapping. Make sure to run the program in the same directory where the trimmed reads (R1 and R2) files are located, no need to run the trimming again.
Reads are mapped (aligned to reference sequences) using the MEM algorithm of BWA and a scoring system to decide which alignment is best with three parameters: match score value (A), mismatch score (B), and gap opening penalty (O).
I want to test out the optimal mapping parameter values before moving forward. Rather than running the dDocent mapping on all the samples, I'm going to save a subset of individuals into a new directory and perform the mapping test on that subset.
Two individuals are selected per bay: one from a population located at the mouth of the bay and one from an upper-bay population, in order to represent a wide spatial gradient.
Sites/Individuals: 
- BIS_NB_1
- PVD_NB_1
- CS_DB_3000
- HC_DB_3031
- HI_CB_3151
- MW_CB_3391
Use samtools flagstats on individual sample files too see how well the mapping worked. I look for which parameters result in the highest percentage of properly paired and lowest percentage of singletons.

Test 1: I'm going to use the default mapping parameters as A = 1, B = 4, and O = 6.
```{bash}
cd /home/ccaillon/RISG_dDocent_working
mkdir mapping_test
cd mapping_test

ln -s ../BIS_NB_1.* .
ln -s ../PVD_NB_1.* .
ln -s ../CS_DB_3000.* .
ln -s ../HC_DB_3031.* .
ln -s ../HI_CB_3151.* .
ln -s ../MW_CB_3391.* .
ln -s ../reference.fasta .
ln -s ../dDocent_ngs .

./dDocent_ngs
```

Use samtools flagstats to investigate bam files
```{bash}
samtools flagstats -@16 BIS_NB_1.F.bam #change the threads with -@16 to make things run faster
samtools flagstats -@16 PVD_NB_1.F.bam
samtools flagstats -@16 CS_DB_3000.F.bam
samtools flagstats -@16 HC_DB_3031.F.bam
samtools flagstats -@16 HI_CB_3151.F.bam
samtools flagstats -@16 MW_CB_3391.F.bam
```

Test 2: Mapping parameter values as A=1, B=3, and O=5 (mostly used in Jonathan Puritz's lab)
```{bash}
cd /home/ccaillon/RISG_dDocent_working/mapping_test
#Run again dDocent in mapping_test directory with the new mapping parameters.
```
Outputs: More passed reads, higher percentage of properly paired reads, and a lower percentage of singletons compared with Test 1 (default parameters).

Test 3: Mapping parameter values as A=2, B=4, and O=6 (optimal parameters of Amy Zyck on NB Seascape Genomics project)
```{bash}
cd /home/ccaillon/RISG_dDocent_working/mapping_test
#Run again dDocent in mapping_test directory with the new mapping parameters.
```
Outputs: Even more passed reads, higher percentage of properly paired reads, and a lower percentage of singletons than Test 2.

Test 4: Mapping parameter values as A=3, B=5, and O=7 (higher values than the default for all three parameters)
```{bash}
cd /home/ccaillon/RISG_dDocent_working/mapping_test
#Run again dDocent in mapping_test directory with the new mapping parameters.
```
Outputs: Less passed reads than Test 2 and Test 3, but higher percentage of properly paired reads and lower percentage of singletons than Test 2 and Test 3.

Test 5: Mapping parameter values as A=2, B=3, and O=5
```{bash}
cd /home/ccaillon/RISG_dDocent_working/mapping_test
#Run again dDocent in mapping_test directory with the new mapping parameters.
```
Outputs: Even less passed reads than Test 4, but highest percentage of properly paired and lowest percentage of singletons among all test.

Test 6: Mapping parameter values as A=2, B=5, and O=7
```{bash}
cd /home/ccaillon/RISG_dDocent_working/mapping_test
#Run again dDocent in mapping_test directory with the new mapping parameters.
```
Outputs: Highest passed reads among all tests, but percentage of properly paired reads and singletons not as good as Test 3.

Conclusion of outputs:
Add table resuming outputs here.
Mapping parameter values A=2, B=4, O=6 is the best option. Even if Test 3 (Amy Zyck's optimal parameters: A=2, B=4, O=6) doesn't top every individual metric, selecting for the best overall compromise across passed reads, properly paired reads, and singleton rates is the right approach for downstream consistency.

Run again dDocent_ngs in the main working directory using the optimal mapping parameter values A=2, B=4, O=6
```{bash}

./dDocent_ngs
```

## SNP Calling

Run dDocent again to call variants using FreeBayes. FreeBayes is a Bayesian-based variant detection program that uses assembled haplotype sequences to simultaneously call SNPs, INDELS, multi-nucleotide polymorphisms (MNPs), and complex events (composite insertion and substitution events) from alignment files (.bam files). At the end, raw SNP calls are concatenated into a single variant call file (VCF) using VCFtools.

```{bash}
cd /home/ccaillon/RISG_dDocent_working
./dDocent_ngs
```

## SNP Filtering

Use PVCF_filter.sh script as a first step filter, it's going to be faster. This script automatically filters genotype calls based on several criteria: genotypes with less than 75% presence across all individuals, a minimum quality score of 20, and a minimum read depth of 5. It also separates nDNA (nuclear DNA) from mtDNA (mitochondrial DNA). Downstream analyses continue with nDNA, separating SNPs and INDELs while retaining only the SNPs.

```{bash}
#We need to run this script within the new directory raw.vcf created by dDocent
cd /home/ccaillon/RISG_dDocent_working/raw.vcf

#Copy the PVCF_filter.sh script from ROD_CADO directory
cp /home/Shared_Data/ROD_CADO/analysis/raw.vcf/PVCF_filter.sh /home/ccaillon/RISG_dDocent_working/raw.vcf/

#Activate conda environment 
conda activate ROD_CADO

#Run
./PVCF_filter.sh TRS 20
```

This script will automatically filter a FreeBayes generated VCF file using criteria related to site depth,
quality versus depth, allelic balance at heterzygous individuals, and paired read representation.
The script assumes that loci and individuals with low call rates (or depth) have already been removed.
